Last week, Anthropic confirmed that it was operating a wet biology lab in the Bay Area where it uses its AI models to run physical experiments. This week, the AI giant announced that this lab has already made what it believes is a big discovery: a new enzyme “system” that has certain “properties reminiscent of CRISPR,” as Anthropic describes it.
CRISPR is a natural immune system used by bacteria to fight off viruses that has become a gene-editing technology widely used by researchers.

Essentially, what Anthropic says it found is a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect and replicate within bacteria. Anthropic’s researchers say this system behaves similarly to CRISPR in that it can “perform operations like cutting, copying, and pasting DNA.”

It will be up to the broader research community to validate how big, or new, this discovery actually is. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei acknowledges that the discovery was based on the work of others and that a team from Stanford previously discovered a system “that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found,” he wrote on X.
But Amodei and Anthropic are not just emphasizing the discovery. They are touting it was found “mostly, though not entirely, by Claude,” the CEO wrote.

On the one hand, that is astounding. This lab was only established this spring (though Anthropic declined to be more specific about how many months it has been open). A discovery in just a few short months would be speedy enough work, but the team said it actually only took Claude 21 hours of concerted effort. Claude searched through data using about 950 agents that burned through 210 million tokens.

Still, the revelation that Anthropic has been conducting biology experiments comes right after AI CEOs, including Amodei, publicly admitted that models have become so capable, and so potentially dangerous, that the industry must slow down and develop safety-testing procedures. This after a couple of his employees publicly said earlier this month that there’s a risk AI could kill us all.

Amodei himself has said one of the things he fears most is that AI could be used for bioterrorism. But he also believes AI will “cure most diseases in 5-10 years,” he wrote. So Anthropic has clearly decided the rewards are worth the risks.
Given that, perhaps the biggest reveal in this news isn’t the discovery itself but that the biology lab hasn’t let Claude loose. The physical experiments were done by humans.

“Our lab, located in the Bay Area, looks like a typical molecular biology lab. We do research that involves only the lower-levels of the biosafety risk level (BSL-1 and BSL-2) and we do not handle pathogens that can infect humans. All of the lab work is performed by human scientists.”

It’s also true that AI-powered biological research is hardly unique to Anthropic. Researchers from Stanford just published a paper on the work they are doing with LLMs and CRISPR. Researchers at UC San Francisco used AI to design enzymes from scratch. Google launched its first AI-powered biology research tool, AlphaFold, back in 2020. So AI has clearly arrived in biological research beyond the AI labs pursuing it themselves.

Yet, Amodei hasn’t ruled out a fully automated biology lab in the future. “Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today,” he said.

上周，Anthropic 证实，它正在湾区运营一个湿生物学实验室，利用其人工智能模型进行物理实验。本周，这家人工智能巨头宣布，该实验室已经取得了它认为的重大发现：一种新的酶“系统”，正如 Anthropic 所描述的那样，它具有某些“让人想起 CRISPR 的特性”。
CRISPR是细菌用来抵抗病毒的天然免疫系统，已成为研究人员广泛使用的基因编辑技术。
从本质上讲，Anthropic 表示，他们发现的是隐藏在噬菌体 DNA 中的一种以前未知的酶系统，噬菌体是感染细菌并在细菌内复制的病毒。 Anthropic 的研究人员表示，该系统的行为与 CRISPR 类似，可以“执行剪切、复制和粘贴 DNA 等操作”。
这将由更广泛的研究界来验证这一发现到底有多大或有多新。 Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 承认，这一发现是基于其他人的工作，斯坦福大学的一个团队之前发现了一个系统，“在某些方面与克劳德发现的系统相似，”他在 X 上写道。
但阿莫代和人类并不仅仅强调这一发现。首席执行官写道，他们宣称该发现“主要是由克劳德发现的，尽管不是全部”。
一方面，这是令人震惊的。该实验室于今年春天才成立（尽管 Anthropic 拒绝透露其已开放几个月的具体信息）。短短几个月的发现已经足够快了，但研究小组表示，实际上只花了克劳德 21 个小时的共同努力。 Claude 使用约 950 个代理搜索数据，销毁了 2.1 亿个代币。
尽管如此，在 Anthropic 一直在进行生物学实验的消息曝光之前，包括 Amodei 在内的人工智能首席执行官公开承认，模型已经变得如此强大，并且具有潜在的危险，以至于该行业必须放慢速度并开发安全测试程序。本月早些时候，他的几名员工公开表示，人工智能有可能杀死我们所有人。
阿莫代本人曾说过，他最担心的事情之一是人工智能可能被用于生物恐怖主义。但他也相信人工智能将“在 5-10 年内治愈大多数疾病”，他写道。因此，Anthropic 明确认为回报值得冒险。
鉴于此，这条新闻中最大的揭露也许不是这一发现本身，而是生物实验室并没有释放克劳德。物理实验是由人类完成的。
“我们的实验室位于湾区，看起来像一个典型的分子生物学实验室。我们所做的研究只涉及生物安全风险级别较低的水平（BSL-1和BSL-2），我们不处理可以感染人类的​​病原体。所有实验室工作都是由人类科学家完成的。”
确实，人工智能驱动的生物学研究并不是 Anthropic 所独有的。斯坦福大学的研究人员刚刚发表了一篇关于他们在法学硕士和 CRISPR 方面所做的工作的论文。加州大学旧金山分校的研究人员利用人工智能从头开始设计酶。谷歌早在 2020 年就推出了首款由人工智能驱动的生物学研究工具 AlphaFold。因此，人工智能显然已经进入了人工智能实验室本身之外的生物学研究领域。
然而，阿莫代并没有排除未来建立全自动生物实验室的可能性。 “最终，克劳德自己甚至有可能通过自主控制实验室设备并采取适当的保障措施来安全地进行实验，但我们今天还没有这样做，”他说。

cards.title: Apple’s iPhone Duo could help fix one of Android’s biggest foldable problems
cards.title_cn: 苹果的 iPhone Duo 可以帮助解决 Android 最大的可折叠问题之一
cards.summary: 【Apple】TL;DR Google’s Android boss says growing interest in foldables could give developers more reason to optimize their apps for larger screens. Some Android apps still haven’t properly adapted to foldable…
fulltext: Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

Android foldables have spent years getting the hardware right, but the app problem has been much harder to shake. Apple’s arrival with the iPhone Duo could finally give developers another reason to take foldable layouts seriously, and Google’s Android boss thinks Android users could benefit too.

Speaking to Tom’s Guide, Android Ecosystem President Sameer Samat said developers see more value in investing in foldables as the form factor becomes more popular. More importantly, he acknowledged that some apps still haven’t made that transition, adding that their developers are either working on it or already in conversations with Google. According to Samat:

App optimization remains one of the biggest weak spots of Android foldables. In our early iPhone Duo hands-on, we found that Apple currently limits multitasking to two apps in landscape on the inner display. But another question stood out: how well will third-party apps adapt to this unusual new screen, and could they ultimately do a better job than their Android counterparts?

Android has certainly been trying to fix its side of the equation. While poor app support helped kill off wide Android foldables, with some apps still letterboxing or stretching instead of properly using the available space, Android 16 began overriding some orientation and resizing restrictions on larger screens. Android 17 doubled down by making adaptive behavior mandatory for apps targeting the latest release. Google Play has also started highlighting apps optimized for larger displays.

Apple’s iPhone Duo could add the ingredient Android hasn’t been able to force: more developer incentive. A bigger foldable audience means more reason to spend time building layouts that properly adapt to changing screen sizes. Samat’s comments suggest Android could benefit from that investment, too.

The Android chief still couldn’t resist a little jab at Apple, boasting that Android is “usually where you see the future first.” He also praised the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which he says he uses for productivity before moving work to his laptop.

Apple may be late to foldables, but its arrival could help Android solve a problem it has struggled with for years: convincing more app developers that foldable-specific experiences are worth the effort.

Android 生态系统总裁 Sameer Samat 在接受 Tom's Guide 采访时表示，随着可折叠设备的外形变得越来越流行，开发人员认为投资可折叠设备具有更大的价值。更重要的是，他承认一些应用程序仍然没有实现这种转变，并补充说他们的开发人员要么正在努力，要么已经在与谷歌进行对话。根据萨马特的说法：
应用程序优化仍然是 Android 可折叠设备的最大弱点之一。在我们早期的 iPhone Duo 实践中，我们发现苹果目前将多任务处理限制为内部显示屏上横向显示的两个应用程序。但另一个问题很突出：第三方应用程序将如何适应这种不寻常的新屏幕，它们最终能否比 Android 同行做得更好？
Android 无疑一直在努力解决自己的问题。虽然糟糕的应用程序支持导致了 Android 可折叠设备的淘汰，一些应用程序仍然采用信箱或拉伸方式，而不是正确使用可用空间，但 Android 16 开始覆盖大屏幕上的一些方向和调整大小限制。 Android 17 使针对最新版本的应用程序强制采用自适应行为，从而加倍努力。 Google Play 也开始突出显示针对更大显示屏进行优化的应用程序。
苹果的 iPhone Duo 可以添加 Android 无法提供的功能：更多的开发者激励。更大的可折叠受众意味着有更多理由花时间构建能够正确适应不断变化的屏幕尺寸的布局。 Samat 的评论表明 Android 也可以从这项投资中受益。
这位 Android 负责人仍然无法抗拒对苹果的攻击，他吹嘘 Android“通常是你首先看到未来的地方”。他还赞扬了 Galaxy Z Fold 8，他说，在将工作转移到笔记本电脑上之前，他用它来提高工作效率。
苹果在可折叠设备上可能姗姗来迟，但它的到来可以帮助Android解决多年来一直困扰的问题：让更多应用程序开发人员相信可折叠设备的特定体验值得付出努力。

fulltext: Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

When Google Vids rolled out in 2024, it was initially intended as a tool for professionals. Even as access expanded beyond Gemini for Workspace customers, the AI-powered video generator remained locked behind Google’s subscription plans. However, Google has been a little more generous in recent months, giving free users a taste earlier this year. Now the company is opening the door for everyone to use Vids with its latest video generation model.

Google has announced that it has integrated its newest AI models into Vids, including Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash-Lite. Anyone with a personal Google or Workspace account can now use the latest Omni model to generate 1080p videos. What’s even better is that you’ll be able to generate videos at no cost.

You can give the tool a try by visiting vids.new on desktop and selecting “Create AI videos.” However, the company doesn’t mention if there are any limits for free users. It only notes that you may want to check out its Google AI plans for more access. Keep in mind that any video you create will have a SynthID digital watermark embedded in its frames.

Along with this announcement, Google revealed that it will soon roll out Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite text-to-speech in Google Vids. This model is designed to turn a script into a voiceover for your generated video. The company says that Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite will support over 100 languages when it rolls out.

Modern life comes with an unending, auto-populating to-do list.

It never ceases to amaze me how I can be doing nothing at all, minding my own business, and suddenly something needs to be taken care of. You’re telling me a tree branch fell in the backyard and now I have to figure out what to do with it? The tree just assigned me homework? Oh, our trash collection company canceled our account out of nowhere and now I have to send email about it? Repeatedly? Totally unfair.

These are the things that we’ve been told for years that AI will help us with. We’ll all have a smart virtual assistant to triage and handle the tedious tasks we’d rather not face. If you believe Meta, that future is available right now in the form of Muse, its AI agent for the masses. I put it to the test doing exactly what it’s advertised to do: taking care of tedious crap I’ve been putting off for ages. And it worked better than I expected — especially when there was a credit card transaction to be made.
It was dizzying watching Marley spin up virtual browser windows chasing down my requests

Marley — one of the suggested names you can give Muse’s avatar — had been pinging me all of last week. It wanted me to know all the ways it could be useful; I was too busy to engage with it. But I sat down with it this week and set it to work on a task. And while it worked on that task, I gave it another. Then another. The thing about AI agents is that they’re most useful when you use them in parallel with each other. Or that’s the theory I was working on. In reality, it was dizzying watching Marley spin up virtual browser windows chasing down my requests. I went with a generically cute snowman-meets-puppy avatar that Meta suggested at setup, and Marley tapped cheerfully on a keyboard as it worked its way through my commands.

In the span of a morning, I gave it the following tasks to help me out with. None of them were critical; mostly they were the kinds of pebble-in-your-shoe annoyances I’d put off for weeks, months, or maybe years. Here’s how it went.
Task: Follow up with the landscaper working on a bid for our backyard renovationEffort rating: Extremely lowTime I have been putting it off: Two weeksWas Marley able to complete it? Yes

I asked Marley to help me nudge the person I’ve been emailing at a local landscaping company. I’m expecting them to price out some yard renovations for us, so Marley requested access to my Gmail to check on the status of that project. It confirmed that more time had passed than the landscaper initially estimated the bid would take, and drafted a rather snippy but wordy email. “Make it shorter,” I said. To be clear: As a rule, I do not use AI writing tools. Definitely not in my work, and not even for email. What’s the point? Just don’t send email if you’re going to have a robot write it. In fact, I think we should abolish email. Anyway, I broke my own rule for testing purposes; hitting send on that message made me cringe.
Task: Buy a replacement steam wand assembly for my espresso machineEffort rating: LowTime I have been putting it off: [redacted] yearsWas Marley able to complete it? Mostly

My Breville Barista Express has held up spectacularly for six years and counting, but it isn’t immune from user error. I took the steam wand apart to clean it a few years back and tore the little silicone washer that goes inside of it. Instead of ordering a new one, I just shoved it back into place and screwed the thing back together. It works okay, but every few months when I’m cleaning the machine it nags at my conscience. It’s probably why the hot water dispenser drips sometimes when I run the steam, too. Ordering a new steam wand assembly costs like 7 bucks and is as difficult as entering my credit card number on Breville’s website. Naturally, I put it off for an unreasonable amount of time.

I opened up my chat with Marley and told it what I needed; it found the part and added it to a shopping cart. I had to finish up the order myself, but it’s done and the part will be here in five to seven business days.

Task: Downgrade my security system account to the cheaper oneEffort rating: Medium (requires a phone call)Time I have been putting it off: A year? Two years???Was Marley able to complete it? Not fully

I approved Marley to log into my account, which also required me to verify my email. While I was making the trip to my inbox I saw I had a follow-up to my follow-up with the landscaper. He was apologetic for the delay and I felt a little bad about the slightly abrupt tone of the email Marley sent. I wrote a friendlier reply the old-fashioned way.

With access to my account, Marley reported back what I already knew: You have to call the company to change your plan. Muse wasn’t able to make a phone call for me, though apparently that ability is in the works. This seems like the logical next frontier for these AI agents, and also a weird future to consider. I call the company and answer a few questions from their robot before I’m routed to a human. No doubt there’s a future soon where Marley talks to the security company’s robot before any human being enters the chat. Or more likely in the short term, a human in a call center talks to the other company’s robot before eventually getting to another human in a call center, which feels even weirder. But surely the end state is that my robot will just talk to their robot and they’ll do business without any intervention at all. Anyway, a nice guy answered and made the change to my account. I think he was real.
Task: Contact a junk removal company to get rid of a fallen tree branch in the backyardEffort rating: MediumTime I have been putting it off: A weekWas Marley able to complete it? Mostly

The tree branch is a real problem I need to deal with. It didn’t do any damage, but it’s big enough that it’ll either take an afternoon to hack apart and haul to the dump or requires a visit from a junk removal service. Marley was most useful here — it set off looking through listings for hauling services and highlighted a few in the area. It asked for my address, phone number, and a photo of the tree limb, and used that information to put together requests for quotes from a couple of companies using online form submissions. I got a text back from one company not long after, and confirmed a time the following day for tree limb removal. Very little was required on my part, and assuming the tree branch is gone by this time tomorrow, I’ll consider this mission accomplished for Muse.
Task: Shop for camping kitchen gear, either as a set or assembled piece by pieceEffort rating: MediumTime I have been putting it off: A few daysWas Marley able to complete it? Yes

If our wallets were already defenseless in the era of one-click checkout, we’re so cooked when AI agent shopping truly arrives. I gave Marley some requirements for my outdoor cooking setup and it set out finding the necessary items. It made an attempt to access Amazon and was roundly blocked, complete with a spicy message about AI agents violating terms of service. Anyway, it found what I was looking for between OXO’s own website and Walmart.

While I was at it, I wanted to add a propane fire pit to the mix. Not for cooking — for ambience and marshmallows. I’d borrowed a couple of different kinds from friends, and after weighing the pros and cons of each with Muse I landed on a LavaBox and a handy carrying case. The grand total for my camp kitchen and burn-ban-safe fire pit: $500! I told Muse we’d have to pump the brakes and spread these purchases out over the winter. It obliged and helped me prioritize what would make sense to buy first and what was likely to go on sale toward the holidays.

In the meantime, I had Marley find and purchase some other espresso machine supplies. I had to connect my credit card via Stripe, but after I’d done that once it became dangerously easy to tell Marley “Go for it” and approve whatever it had just put in my shopping cart. I watched it fill in my address details in the virtual browser window and confirmation emails started filing into my inbox. Marley did a little shopping around to find slightly better prices, and I didn’t buy anything egregious — just some descaling powder and water filters. It also did the math to calculate whether powdered Dezcal would be a better value than the liquid stuff (way better, not surprisingly). But it is shockingly easy to spend money when a cute little guy is running around the internet with your credit card.
It is shockingly easy to spend money when a cute little guy is running around the internet with your credit card

There’s a danger in overcommitting yourself when you feel like these AI tools are speeding you up. In a few cases, Muse helped me get started by putting the details I needed in front of my face. I had the phone number for the home security company at hand, as well as the name of my current plan and the one I wanted to downgrade to. Getting that little speed bump out of the way was what I needed, I guess. But the dirty secret of productivity hacks is that doing more stuff often doesn’t feel like things are being removed from your plate; somehow it just invites more tasks.

If you’re willing to give a lot of information and trust to Meta — a massive caveat! — Muse can genuinely help you get things done. I’d been using it for all of 40 minutes and already given it my full name, address, credit card number, a photo of my backyard, and the credentials for my home security account login. Going great, I’d say! If AI decides to kill us all I just secured my spot at the front of the line. Meta of course says that all of these details are stored securely, Marley allegedly can’t even see them, etc., but still. Unsettling.

But I think the underlying question we need to ask ourselves as we enter the era of AI agents is what we do with the time we’re supposedly freeing up. Will we use it to take on more commitments? And then ultimately feel overwhelmed again when the to-do list keeps piling up? After a morning crossing items off my list with Marley, I didn’t spend the hours that followed doing anything consequential. In fact, I spent that time chatting with Marley, seeking reassurance about the direction of the yard project and brainstorming fall camping trips I probably won’t take. It’s a gorgeous day outside, the kind we really can’t take for granted in late September, and I wish I’d spent that time outdoors rather than inside talking to a robot, cute little guy or otherwise.

fulltext_cn: ﻿Muse 在我的待办事项清单上做得不错，但是使用信用卡真的很方便吗？
现代生活伴随着无止尽的、自动填充的待办事项清单。
我总是感到惊讶，我什么都不做，只顾自己的事，突然间需要处理一些事情。你是在告诉我后院有一根树枝掉下来了，现在我必须弄清楚如何处理它？树刚刚给我布置了作业？哦，我们的垃圾收集公司突然取消了我们的帐户，现在我必须发送电子邮件吗？反复？完全不公平。
多年来我们一直被告知人工智能将帮助我们解决这些问题。我们都会有一个智能虚拟助手来分类和处理我们不想面对的繁琐任务。如果你相信 Meta，那么这个未来现在就以 Muse 的形式出现，它是面向大众的人工智能代理。我对它进行了测试，完全按照它所宣传的那样做：处理我已经拖延了很长时间的乏味废话。它的效果比我预期的要好——尤其是当需要进行信用卡交易时。
看着马利旋转虚拟浏览器窗口追逐我的请求真是令人眼花缭乱

马利（Marley）——你可以给缪斯头像起的建议名字之一——上周一直在给我打电话。它想让我知道它的所有用途；我太忙了，没时间参与其中。但这周我坐下来研究它并让它完成一项任务。当它完成这项任务时，我给了它另一个任务。然后是另一个。人工智能代理的特点是，当你并行使用它们时，它们是最有用的。或者这就是我正在研究的理论。事实上，看着马利旋转虚拟浏览器窗口追逐我的请求真是令人眼花缭乱。我选择了 Meta 在设置时建议的一个可爱的雪人与小狗的化身，马利在键盘上愉快地敲击着我的命令。
在一个早上的时间里，我给了它以下任务来帮助我完成。他们中没有一个人是持批评态度的。大多数都是我推迟数周、数月甚至数年的麻烦事。事情是这样的。
任务：跟进园林设计师对我们后院翻新的投标工作评级：极低我推迟的时间：两周马利能够完成它吗？是的

我请马利帮我推动我一直在当地一家园林绿化公司发电子邮件的人。我希望他们能为我们定价一些院子装修的费用，所以马利请求访问我的 Gmail 以检查该项目的状态。它证实，所花费的时间比园林设计师最初估计的投标时间要长，并起草了一封相当尖刻但冗长的电子邮件。 “把它缩短一点，”我说。需要明确的是：一般来说，我不使用人工智能写作工具。绝对不会出现在我的工作中，甚至不会出现在电子邮件中。有什么意义？如果您要让机器人来写电子邮件，请不要发送电子邮件。事实上，我认为我们应该废除电子邮件。无论如何，出于测试目的，我打破了自己的规则；点击发送该消息让我感到畏缩。
任务：为我的浓缩咖啡机购买一个替换蒸汽棒组件努力程度：低时间我一直推迟它：[编辑]年马利能够完成它吗？大多

我的 Breville Barista Express 已经连续六年运行良好，而且还在持续增长，但它也不能免受用户错误的影响。几年前，我把蒸汽棒拆开来清洁它，并撕坏了里面的小硅胶垫圈。我没有订购新的，而是将其推回原位，然后将其重新拧紧在一起。它工作得很好，但每隔几个月，当我清洁机器时，它就会困扰我的良心。这可能就是为什么当我运行蒸汽时热水器有时会滴水的原因。订购一个新的蒸汽棒组件大约需要 7 美元，而且就像在 Breville 网站上输入我的信用卡号码一样困难。自然地，我把它推迟了一段不合理的时间。
我打开了与 Marley 的聊天窗口并告诉它我需要什么；它找到了该零件并将其添加到购物车中。我必须自己完成订单，但订单已经完成，零件将在五到七个工作日内到达。
任务：将我的安全系统帐户降级到更便宜的一个 努力程度：中（需要打电话） 我推迟的时间：一年？两年？？？马利能完成吗？不完全
我批准 Marley 登录我的帐户，这也要求我验证我的电子邮件。当我前往收件箱时，我看到我与园艺师的后续行动有后续行动。他对延迟表示歉意，而我对马利发送的电子邮件中略显唐突的语气感到有点难过。我用老式的方式写了一个更友好的回复。

通过访问我的帐户，马利报告了我已经知道的情况：您必须致电公司更改您的计划。 Muse 无法帮我打电话，尽管显然这种能力正在开发中。这似乎是这些人工智能代理合乎逻辑的下一个前沿领域，也是一个需要考虑的奇怪的未来。我打电话给该公司，回答了他们机器人提出的几个问题，然后才被转接给人工接听。毫无疑问，不久的将来，马利会在任何人进入聊天之前与安全公司的机器人进行对话。或者更有可能的是，在短期内，呼叫中心的一个人与另一家公司的机器人交谈，然后最终与呼叫中心的另一个人交谈，这感觉更奇怪。但最终状态肯定是我的机器人只会与他们的机器人交谈，而他们将在没有任何干预的情况下开展业务。不管怎样，一个好人回答了我的问题并更改了我的帐户。我认为他是真实的。
任务：联系垃圾清除公司清除后院倒下的树枝努力程度：中等时间我一直推迟：一周马利能完成吗？大多

树枝是我需要处理的一个现实问题。它没有造成任何损坏，但它足够大，要么需要一个下午才能分解并拖到垃圾场，要么需要垃圾清除服务人员上门。马利在这里最有用——它开始查找运输服务列表，并突出显示了该地区的一些服务。它询问了我的地址、电话号码和树枝的照片，并利用这些信息通过在线提交表格将几家公司的报价请求汇总在一起。不久后，我收到一家公司的回复短信，并确定了第二天拆除树枝的时间。我几乎不需要做任何事情，假设明天这个时候树枝已经消失了，我会认为缪斯的任务已经完成。
任务：购买野营厨房用具，无论是成套的还是逐件组装的 努力程度：中等 我一直在拖延时间：几天 马利能够完成它吗？是的
如果说我们的钱包在一键结账时代已经毫无防备，那么当人工智能代购真正到来时，我们就已经熟透了。我向马利提出了一些关于我的户外烹饪设置的要求，并开始寻找必要的物品。它尝试访问亚马逊，但遭到全面封锁，并附有一条有关人工智能代理违反服务条款的辛辣信息。不管怎样，它在 OXO 自己的网站和沃尔玛之间找到了我要找的东西。
当我在做的时候，我想在混合物中添加一个丙烷火坑。不是为了烹饪，而是为了氛围和棉花糖。我从朋友那里借了几种不同的产品，在与 Muse 权衡了每种产品的优缺点后，我最终选择了 LavaBox 和一个方便的手提箱。我的营地厨房和防烧火坑的总计：500 美元！我告诉缪斯，我们必须踩刹车，将这些采购分散到整个冬天。它帮助我优先考虑哪些产品是值得首先购买的，哪些产品可能会在假期期间打折。

与此同时，我让马利找到并购买了一些其他浓缩咖啡机用品。我必须通过 Stripe 连接我的信用卡，但是一旦我这样做了，告诉 Marley“去做吧”并批准它刚刚放入我的购物车的任何东西就变得非常容易了。我看着它在虚拟浏览器窗口中填写我的地址详细信息，确认电子邮件开始进入我的收件箱。马利四处逛逛，找到了稍微便宜一点的价格，我没有买任何过分的东西——只是一些除垢粉和滤水器。它还进行了数学计算，计算粉末状的 Dezcal 是否比液体的更有价值（更好，毫不奇怪）。但当一个可爱的小家伙拿着你的信用卡在互联网上跑来跑去时，花钱是非常容易的。
当一个可爱的小家伙拿着你的信用卡在互联网上跑来跑去时，花钱真是太容易了

当你觉得这些人工智能工具正在加速你的速度时，过度投入是危险的。在某些情况下，Muse 通过将我需要的细节放在我面前来帮助我开始。我手头有家庭安全公司的电话号码，以及我当前计划的名称和我想要降级的计划的名称。我想，把那个小减速带移开就是我所需要的。但生产力黑客的肮脏秘密是，做更多的事情通常不会让人感觉事情被从你的盘子里删除；相反，你会感觉事情已经从你的盘子里被删除了。不知怎的，它只会带来更多的任务。
如果您愿意向 Meta 提供大量信息并信任它——这是一个巨大的警告！ — Muse 可以真正帮助您完成任务。我已经使用了它 40 分钟，并且已经向它提供了我的全名、地址、信用卡号、我后院的照片以及我的家庭安全帐户登录凭据。我想说，进展顺利！如果人工智能决定杀死我们所有人，我就确保了我在队伍前面的位置。 Meta 当然说所有这些细节都被安全地存储，据称马利甚至看不到它们等等，但仍然如此。令人不安。

但我认为，当我们进入人工智能代理时代时，我们需要问自己的根本问题是我们如何利用我们应该腾出的时间。我们会用它来承担更多承诺吗？当待办事项清单不断堆积时，最终再次感到不知所措？在一个早上与马利划掉清单上的项目之后，我没有花接下来的几个小时做任何重要的事情。事实上，我花了这段时间与马利聊天，寻求院子项目方向的保证，并集思广益我可能不会参加秋季露营旅行。外面是美好的一天，九月下旬我们真的不能认为这是理所当然的，我希望我在户外度过这段时间，而不是在里面与机器人、可爱的小家伙或其他人交谈。

cards.summary: 【Android Authority】TL;DR YouTube is turning its earlier Custom Feed experiment into a full feature that lets you build recommendation feeds with conversational prompts. You can save multiple feeds for different interest…
fulltext: Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

YouTube’s Home tab has always had a funny way of overreacting. Watch one random woodworking video, and suddenly the algorithm can decide you’ve found your new life’s calling. Last year, YouTube started testing a way to fight that problem by letting some users tell an AI chatbot what they actually wanted to see. Now that experiment is growing up, with YouTube officially announcing Custom Feeds, giving viewers a more direct way to build separate recommendation feeds around specific interests, routines, or moods.

The original test added a “Your Custom Feed” chip beside Home for select users. You could prompt YouTube to adjust what appeared there, essentially correcting the recommendation algorithm instead of waiting for your watch history to do the job.

The version YouTube has just announced goes further. Instead of one experimental feed, viewers can create and save multiple Custom Feeds using conversational prompts. You could make one for evening wind-down with long documentaries, another for discovering new DIY creators, or something as specific as podcasts for a 30-minute commute.

Those feeds will live on the Homepage and automatically refresh with new recommendations. That separation could be the biggest win. Rather than letting every passing curiosity muddy your main recommendations, you can keep different interests in their own lanes.
YouTube says Custom Feeds are coming this fall to users in the US across the web, mobile apps, and TVs, turning last year’s limited experiment into a much broader feature.

Custom Feeds aren’t the only viewer-focused upgrade announced today. After rolling out to mobile users, YouTube is now expanding Ask YouTube with shopping-focused questions, follow-ups, and organized product comparisons, including voice interaction on TVs.

Made On YouTube 2026 also included plenty for creators, including conversational editing, video A/B testing, improved likeness detection, and new Live tools. But for everyday viewers, Custom Feeds could be the change that makes YouTube’s recommendations feel less like a guess and more like something you deliberately shaped.

cards.title_cn: 在 GitHub Copilot 应用程序中呈现巨大的拉取请求
cards.summary: 【GitHub】Broad refactors and migrations often have to land as one change. Stacked pull requests are a great way to split work into smaller changes, which makes reviews easier and helps teams ship with less ris…
fulltext: Broad refactors and migrations often have to land as one change.

Stacked pull requests are a great way to split work into smaller changes, which makes reviews easier and helps teams ship with less risk. But some changes, like this one, can’t be split cleanly. That leaves you with a single pull request that can get very large, and the review conversation causes it to grow.
The review experience needs to remain fast and smooth even when the diff and its conversation are enormous. In the GitHub Copilot app, we rebuilt the pull request view with that requirement in mind.

To see how far that goes, we opened the biggest pull request we could find: an open source one with 2,200 files, over a million changed lines, and more than 400 inline review comments. Here’s how we made even this extreme pull request performant.
Rendering a large diff at speed is well-understood: virtualize the rows, keep the mounted DOM small, and lean on the fact that every row is a line of code at a known height.

Comments are the hard part. A comment’s height depends on how its markdown wraps, the expandable sections, whether there’s a reply box in it, and whether its images have loaded yet. You find all of that out at render time. This forces a different architecture.
Three problems:
The first step is to understand the geometry that makes a code-only diff fast. Once comments enter the picture, that geometry is no longer enough.

You cannot put a million DOM nodes on a page. The standard answer is virtualization: mount only the rows that are on screen, plus a small margin, and recycle those same DOM elements as the user scrolls. The list behaves as if all million rows exist. The scrollbar is the right size, scroll-to-row works. But only about 100 rows are ever real at once.

For this illusion to hold, something has to supply the geometry. The scrollbar height is the sum of all row heights. The position of row N is the sum of the heights of the rows above it. Jumping to a row, drawing the scrollbar, deciding what’s on screen, it’s all arithmetic over a table of heights. You can build that table from estimates and correct it as rows get measured, and general-purpose variable-height virtualizers do exactly that.
But if every row is a line of code at a known font size, you don’t have to. You can compute the whole table up front and it never changes, so there’s nothing to correct later.
Call this the “all heights known before paint” contract. Our diff surface is built around it:
None of it scales badly, because no per-frame work grows with the total row count. On pure code this design is the right one, and we kept all of it.
Now put a review thread in the middle of the diff. How tall is it?
You don’t know, and you can’t know without rendering it. Its height depends on things that only exist at render time, and they can keep changing after first paint:

The obvious answer is to reserve a fixed-height slot for each comment, sized by an estimator. It falls apart on a big pull request. An estimator that’s right on average is still wrong at the extremes. It over-reserves most comments, leaving gaps of whitespace, and under-reserves the expensive ones, which clip or sprout a nested scrollbar. If you measure the real height after paint and write it back into the shared offset table, everything below moves, while the user is already scrolling. That’s a scroll jump, and on a big pull request it’s a large one.

So comments need a different contract. “All heights known before paint” is unachievable for this content. What we could promise instead: heights are bounded, measured lazily, and corrections are small and anchored to whatever the user is looking at.
The idea that made this tractable was to stop forcing one geometry to serve both kinds of content. We split the document’s height into two independent domains:
Code geometry keeps the original world. It’s deterministic, prefix-summed, exact, never rebuilt when a comment resizes.

Dynamic block geometry covers everything whose height we can’t predict, such as review threads, drafts, and reply composers. Each one is a block identified by what it is rather than where it currently sits. It has a stable key that survives its content loading, and it’s anchored to a file, line and side rather than to a pixel coordinate, so a reflow can’t lose track of it. We also keep a fingerprint of everything that could change the block’s height: its content, whether a <details> is open, whether a composer is active. And we record the width it was last measured at, rounded into buckets, so an ordinary window resize doesn’t invalidate every measurement in the document.

A block’s effective height is then simple: the measured height if we have a valid one, a cached height if the fingerprint and width still match, and the estimate otherwise. Those heights live in their own index, separate from the code rows, so a resizing comment never forces the code geometry to be rebuilt. And the number of blocks is bounded by comments, not by rows. A few thousand blocks is fine, as long as first paint never mounts or measures all of them at once.
This part took the longest to get right, because our first design was wrong in an instructive way.

The obvious way to measure dynamic content is one ResizeObserver per block, which watches the element and writes its measured height back into the layout whenever it changes. This is what we designed and then rejected during performance hardening. It is the feedback loop that big virtualized surfaces have to avoid. An observer that writes a height back into the layout of the element it’s watching can retrigger itself, and the cost grows with every mounted block.
What shipped instead is a single idle- and scroll-gated measurement pass, held to the same discipline as the deterministic side:
When a measured height differs from its estimate, the scrollbar arithmetic changes, and the naive result is that the viewport jumps. The fix is to correct by identity rather than by pixel:
Plus a few rules that keep it from feeling wrong:

That last rule has a sharp edge, and it bit us. “Don’t correct while the user is scrolling” was implemented as a guard on the last observed scroll, and programmatic scrolls refreshed that timestamp too. Toggling the file-tree sidebar changes the width of the diff pane. With line wrapping on, every wrapped line above you reflows to a different number of visual lines, the whole coordinate space shifts, and the surface emits a small scroll of its own as it settles. The guard read that as “the user just scrolled” and skipped the very correction that was supposed to keep your place, so the file you were reading drifted off screen. The fix was to tell user scrolls apart from ones the surface caused itself. Any “is the user interacting?” check has to be one your own side effects can’t satisfy.
So corrections stay small, they reuse measurements we already have, and they follow whatever you’re looking at.

A diff surface can only be as fast as the data feeding it, and three habits from that side of the work shaped what the UI could do. The first is stream structure before content. The diff is requested incrementally, so the file tree and metadata paint while the document is still loading, and the full set of review threads is resolved up front rather than trickling in. The second is defer per-item work until something needs it. Syntax highlighting runs off the main thread, so rows appear as plain text immediately and get colored when the results arrive. Highlighting improves the surface instead of blocking the scroll. Large markdown bodies and suggested-change context work the same way: nothing is built until it approaches the viewport.

The third habit is about which costs are worth keeping. Releasing a diff document when you navigate away is the right default. These documents are large, and holding on to every one you’ve visited is how a long session ends up eating memory. But pull request metadata persists, so the shell around the diff, the header and the file tree, repaints instantly when you go back, and then sits there for several seconds waiting for a diff it had complete moments ago. An instantly-drawn shell around an empty diff looks broken, even though you’re waiting less time overall. So the policy stayed and we added a cache: keep the last few diffs resident, evict anything beyond that, and let the background refresh notice when one has gone stale.

Almost every bug in this project was invisible until it wasn’t, and reproducing one by hand is miserable. A typical report reads: “a strip of whitespace appears below some comments, but only sometimes, only on big pull requests, and it heals if you scroll past and back.” You can’t debug that by staring at the screen, so we built tooling to debug it mechanically.

The naive workflow is to sprinkle console.log calls, exercise the flow by hand, copy the output, paste it to someone (or something) that can analyze it, delete the logs, and repeat. It’s slow, it needs a human in the loop, and worst of all you end up measuring your own hand-rolled instrumentation rather than the app’s real behavior.
So the surface carries permanent, structured probes for its own invariants. They’re plain questions it answers about itself on every render:

These are the objective pass/fail signals, and they’re asserted as budgets in an end-to-end test against a synthetic many-comment huge-pull-request fixture. CI can now tell us whether the surface is healthy.
The centerpiece was an autonomous change → measure → improve loop. Two lanes:

A headless probe lane ran a declarative flow (open a pull request, scroll to a fraction, toggle a details block, resize the window) against a mock server, reading the app’s own production instrumentation: React render counts, the performance timeline, and a requestAnimationFrame sampler for jank. It did the whole instrument, drive, collect, analyze, rank cycle by itself and printed the bottlenecks in order. Because the flow is just JSON handed to the probe at runtime, an agent could profile any flow by describing it in plain English, without editing a line of source.

An autopilot drove the actual desktop app through the huge-pull-request flow, unattended, on a loop: first cold, with comments still skeletons, then warm, with comments loaded, toggling <details> blocks, opening and cancelling reply composers, collapsing and expanding files, toggling the sidebar tree, sweeping deep into the file list, resizing the window. Every measurement was mirrored to the app’s on-disk log, so an agent could read runtime behavior with nobody at the keyboard. Each sample carried a health signal, and that was the objective check. A warm sample counted as healthy only if there were no unfilled gaps between comments, no comment blocks left blank, and real thread content actually mounted, across the entire scroll range, deep-file sweep included.
The loop we ran was:

Reviewing a pull request this large used to mean one of two things: waiting, or giving up and reading it somewhere else. A review isn’t a document with known dimensions. It’s a conversation that changes shape while you’re reading it, and the surface underneath has to be built for that from the start rather than patched into it afterwards.

The result is a pull request view where a million-line diff with hundreds of threaded comments opens, scrolls, and behaves like a normally sized pull request. Comments render in full instead of clipping into a scrollable box. Expanding a collapsed section moves the code below it and nothing else. Coming back to a pull request you just left puts you where you were.
If you review code for a living, it’s worth feeling the difference on a pull request you already know is painful. Open the worst one you’ve got.

cards.summary_cn: 【GitHub】广泛的重构和迁移通常必须作为一项变更来实施。堆叠拉取请求是将工作拆分为更小的更改的好方法，这使得审查更容易，并帮助团队以更少的风险进行交付……
fulltext_cn: 广泛的重构和迁移通常必须作为一项变更来实施。
堆叠拉取请求是将工作拆分为更小的更改的好方法，这使得审查更容易，并帮助团队降低风险。但有些变化，比如这个，不能完全分开。这给你留下了一个可能变得非常大的拉取请求，而审查对话会导致它增长。
即使差异及其对话巨大，审阅体验也需要保持快速和流畅。在 GitHub Copilot 应用程序中，我们根据该要求重建了拉取请求视图。
为了看看能走多远，我们提出了我们能找到的最大的拉取请求：一个开源请求，包含 2,200 个文件、超过一百万行的更改行以及超过 400 条内联审核评论。以下是我们如何使这种极端的拉取请求变得高性能。
快速渲染大差异是很好理解的：虚拟化行，保持安装的 DOM 小，并依靠每行都是已知高度的一行代码这一事实。
评论是最难的部分。评论的高度取决于其降价方式、可扩展部分、是否有回复框以及图像是否已加载。您可以在渲染时发现所有这些。这迫使我们采用不同的架构。
三个问题：
第一步是了解使仅代码差异快速进行的几何结构。一旦评论出现，几何图形就不再足够了。
您无法在一个页面上放置一百万个 DOM 节点。标准答案是虚拟化：仅安装屏幕上的行，加上一个小边距，并在用户滚动时回收这些相同的 DOM 元素。该列表的行为就像所有百万行都存在一样。滚动条大小合适，滚动到行有效。但同时只有大约 100 行是真实的。
为了维持这种错觉，必须有某种东西来提供几何形状。滚动条高度是所有行高度的总和。第 N 行的位置是其上方各行的高度之和。跳到一行，绘制滚动条，决定屏幕上显示的内容，这都是高度表上的算术。您可以根据估计构建该表，并在测量行时对其进行更正，通用可变高度虚拟器正是这样做的。
但如果每一行都是已知字体大小的一行代码，则不必这样做。您可以预先计算整个表格，并且它永远不会改变，因此以后无需更正。
将此称为“油漆前已知的所有高度”合同。我们的 diff 表面是围绕它构建的：
它们的扩展性都不会很差，因为每帧的工作不会随着总行数的增长而增长。在纯代码上，这种设计是正确的，我们保留了所有它。
现在将审查线程放在差异的中间。它有多高？
你不知道，如果不渲染它你就无法知道。它的高度取决于仅在渲染时存在的东西，并且它们可以在第一次绘制后不断变化：
显而易见的答案是为每个评论保留一个固定高度的插槽，由估算器调整大小。它在一个大的拉取请求中崩溃了。平均而言正确的估计器在极端情况下仍然是错误的。它过度保留了大多数注释，留下了空白，而保留了昂贵的注释，这些注释会剪切或产生嵌套滚动条。如果您在绘制后测量实际高度并将其写回到共享偏移表中，则下面的所有内容都会移动，而用户已经在滚动。这是一个滚动跳转，对于一个大的拉取请求来说，这是一个很大的跳转。
所以评论需要不同的合同。对于此内容来说，“绘制之前已知的所有高度”是无法实现的。我们可以承诺的是：高度是有界的，延迟测量，修正很小，并且锚定到用户正在看的任何东西。
使这种情况变得容易处理的想法是停止强迫一种几何体服务于两种内容。我们将文档的高度分为两个独立的域：
代码几何保留了原始世界。它是确定性的、前缀求和的、精确的，当评论大小调整时永远不会重建。

动态块几何形状涵盖了我们无法预测高度的所有内容，例如审阅线程、草稿和回复编辑器。每个块都是一个块，通过它的内容而不是它当前所在的位置来识别。它有一个稳定的密钥，可以在内容加载后继续存在，并且它锚定到文件、行和侧面而不是像素坐标，因此回流不会丢失它的跟踪。我们还保留了所有可能改变块高度的指纹：它的内容、<details>是否打开、作曲家是否处于活动状态。我们记录最后测量的宽度，四舍五入到桶中，因此普通的窗口大小调整不会使文档中的每个测量值无效。
块的有效高度很简单：如果我们有有效的高度，则测量高度；如果指纹和宽度仍然匹配，则缓存高度，否则估计。这些高度位于它们自己的索引中，与代码行分开，因此调整大小注释永远不会强制重建代码几何图形。块的数量由注释限制，而不是由行限制。几千块就可以了，只要第一次油漆不会同时安装或测量所有块即可。
这部分花了最长的时间才完成，因为我们的第一个设计在启发性方面是错误的。
测量动态内容的明显方法是每个块一个 ResizeObserver，它监视元素并在元素发生变化时将其测量的高度写回到布局中。这是我们设计的，然后在性能强化过程中​​被拒绝的。这是大型虚拟化表面必须避免的反馈循环。将高度写回其正在观察的元素的布局中的观察者可以重新触发自身，并且成本随着每个安装的块而增加。
相反，提供的是单个空闲和滚动门控测量通道，与确定性方面遵循相同的规则：
当测量的高度与其估计的高度不同时，滚动条算术会发生变化，并且简单的结果是视口跳跃。解决方法是通过身份而不是像素进行纠正：
再加上一些避免感觉错误的规则：

最后一条规则有锋利的一面，它咬住了我们。 “用户滚动时不要纠正”被实现为对最后观察到的滚动的保护，并且编程滚动也刷新了该时间戳。切换文件树侧边栏会更改差异窗格的宽度。打开换行后，您上方的每条换行都会回流到不同数量的视线，整个坐标空间会发生变化，并且表面在稳定时会发出自己的小滚动。警卫将其解读为“用户刚刚滚动”，并跳过了本应保留您位置的更正，因此您正在阅读的文件偏离了屏幕。解决方法是告诉用户滚动与表面本身引起的滚动分开。任何“用户正在交互吗？”检查必须是你自己的副作用无法满足的一项。
因此，修正量很小，它们会重复使用我们已有的测量结果，并且它们会遵循您所看到的任何内容。

差异表面的速度只能与输入数据的速度一样快，而工作方面的三个习惯决定了 UI 的功能。第一个是内容之前的流结构。差异是增量请求的，因此文件树和元数据在文档仍在加载时绘制，并且全套审阅线程会预先解决，而不是慢慢加入。第二个是推迟每个项目的工作，直到有需要为止。语法突出显示在主线程之外运行，因此行会立即显示为纯文本，并在结果到达时变为彩色。突出显示可以改善表面而不是阻碍滚动。大型降价正文和建议更改上下文的工作方式相同：在接近视口之前不会构建任何内容。

第三个习惯是关于哪些成本值得保留。当您离开时释放 diff 文档是正确的默认设置。这些文档很大，并且保留您访问过的每一个文档都是长时间会话最终会消耗内存的原因。但是拉取请求元数据仍然存在，因此当您返回时，围绕差异、标头和文件树的 shell 会立即重新绘制，然后在那里等待几秒钟，等待刚刚完成的差异。即使您总体等待的时间较短，围绕空差异的即时绘制外壳看起来也已损坏。因此，策略保留下来，我们添加了一个缓存：保留最后几个差异，驱逐除此之外的任何内容，并在某个差异过时时让后台刷新通知。
这个项目中的几乎每个错误都是不可见的，直到它消失为止，并且手动重现一个错误是痛苦的。一份典型的报告写道：“一些评论下面会出现一条空白，但只是有时，只有在大的拉取请求上，如果你滚动过去和向后，它就会消失。”你无法通过盯着屏幕来调试它，因此我们构建了工具来机械地调试它。
简单的工作流程是散布 console.log 调用，手动执行流程，复制输出，将其粘贴到可以分析它的某人（或某物），删除日志，然后重复。它很慢，需要有人参与循环，最糟糕的是你最终测量的是自己的手动仪器，而不是应用程序的真实行为。
因此，表面带有永久的、结构化的探针来检测其自身的不变量。它们是它在每次渲染时回答自己的简单问题：
这些是客观的通过/失败信号，它们在针对合成的许多评论的巨大拉动请求固定装置的端到端测试中被断言为预算。 CI 现在可以告诉我们表面是否健康。
核心是自主改变→措施→改进循环。两车道：

无头探测通道针对模拟服务器运行声明性流程（打开拉取请求、滚动到分数、切换细节块、调整窗口大小），读取应用程序自己的生产仪器：React 渲染计数、性能时间线和用于卡顿的 requestAnimationFrame 采样器。它自己完成了整个仪器、驱动、收集、分析、排序循环，并按顺序打印瓶颈。由于流只是在运行时传递给探测器的 JSON，因此代理可以通过用简单的英语描述来分析任何流，而无需编辑一行源代码。

cards.title: Data centers are black boxes, but California wants to change that
cards.title_cn: 数据中心是黑匣子，但加州希望改变这一现状
cards.summary: 【The Verge】California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a slate of bills on Monday that could finally give communities better data - and more say - on how data centers impact their electricity bills and water supply. As…
fulltext: New legislation will finally force data centers to disclose more information about how much water and electricity they use in California.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a slate of bills on Monday that could finally give communities better data — and more say — on how data centers impact their electricity bills and water supply.

As data centers invade a growing number of communities across the US, they’ve triggered protests over how the infrastructure underpinning AI might stress power grids and local water systems. That’s fueled partly by concerns about how difficult it is to see just how much electricity or water they’re actually gobbling up. California’s new disclosure rules won’t offer a full picture, but starting next year, data center operators will have to start sharing some of these details. The transparency will help scientists and the public see whether data centers are raising bills, draining dwindling resources, and making good on sustainability commitments.

“It’s extremely frustrating to try to understand basic information,” says Mark Specht, senior manager for the climate and energy program at the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS). “There’s a lot of hype about data centers right now … It doesn’t help that we just don’t have basic facts about what’s happening with them to try to understand how much of a problem they are.”
“It’s extremely frustrating”

The seven bills Newsom signed go beyond requiring disclosures. Senate Bill 886, Assembly Bill 2383, and Senate Bill 1168 direct the California Public Utilities Commission to create separate power rates for data centers to recoup the costs of connecting such power-hungry facilities to the grid. That’s supposed to prevent data centers from passing on the costs to other consumers of new infrastructure built to satisfy their energy demand. On top of that, AB 2383 also pushes data centers to use more renewable energy.

The rest of the legislation grapples with the enormous gaps the public has when it comes to how data centers impact surrounding communities and the environment. AB 1577 requires monthly reporting on data centers’ energy consumption. AB 2619 and AB 2469 require water disclosures, and the latter also makes data center operators responsible for covering the costs of infrastructure upgrades needed to serve them. And SB 887 eliminates categorical exemptions from the California Environmental Quality Act for data centers, ensuring that they’re subject to environmental review.
“As scientists, when we went to research state offers in California, I was kind of dismayed by the lack of information that there was to work with. And so I’m happy [AB 1577] passed,” Specht says.

Specht co-authored a fact sheet this year on how data centers could impact the power grid and utility rates in California. It describes one scenario where several factors drive up costs for Californians: ballooning electricity demand; a need for expensive new infrastructure to connect data centers to high-voltage transmission systems; and the risk of overbuilding if the AI bubble pops and data centers don’t end up using as much electricity as projected, leaving other utility customers to foot the bill .
A different scenario shows data centers could actually lower electricity costs

On the other hand, a different scenario shows data centers could actually lower electricity costs. Electricity rates include fixed costs for grid maintenance, so spreading those costs across more customers can bring bills down for everyone. The catch is that the potential savings depend on data centers contributing to costs across the distribution system that serves smaller customers at lower voltages. Large data centers often avoid these costs by connecting instead to the transmission system, which carries high-voltage electricity.

Without more information, it’s impossible to say which scenario is taking shape in California. “I wouldn’t say definitively that data centers have increased the cost [of electricity],” Specht says. “It’s possible they may even have brought them down some already, I just don’t think we have the numbers to demonstrate it.”

Even if data centers aren’t having much effect on electricity rates yet, that’s likely to change as their power needs grow, Specht adds — making it all the more important to see how much energy they’re using. “It’s just about getting ahead of it before we all start feeling it,” he tells The Verge.

Data centers’ water use has been just as opaque. While studying the impact of data centers on water-stressed communities in California, researchers from Santa Clara University recently contacted every water provider in districts housing data centers. Citing privacy regulations, the providers in every district refused to share data on how much water data centers use. The researchers also discovered that very few data centers in the state had environmental impact reports available to the public.
The laws still leave big gaps in what data centers need to report

That dearth of information is even more concerning considering what the researchers were able to find. As AI drives the development of hyperscale data centers, these facilities are moving farther from more affluent urban areas into more rural areas where small water systems and lower-income communities may have more difficulty coping with the added demand.

The laws still leave big gaps in what data centers need to report. Specifically, AB 2619 and AB 2469 only require companies to make water disclosures when applying for permits or getting a business license, so we won’t know how much water they’re actually using from year to year. The year in which they share their water use could be particularly wet or cool, not necessarily reflecting how much water the facility needs when it’s hotter and drier. It also makes it difficult to see if a data center’s consumption is growing or if a company is following through on its sustainability goals.

Still, “This is in many ways a step in the right direction. It’s signaling to the industry that people are paying attention, that lawmakers are paying attention,” says Iris Stewart-Frey, the lead author of that water report and a professor of environmental science at Santa Clara University.
She notes that Newsom actually vetoed a similar water disclosure bill last year, but that data centers have become a bigger concern for the public since then.
“The whole AI wave is not a force of nature, it’s not a hurricane,” she says. “This is something that we can actually regulate.”

fulltext_cn: 新的立法最终将迫使数据中心披露更多关于他们在加州使用了多少水和电的信息。
加州州长加文·纽瑟姆周一签署了一系列法案，最终可以为社区提供更好的数据——以及更多的发言权——关于数据中心如何影响他们的电费和供水。
随着数据中心侵入美国越来越多的社区，它们引发了人们对支持人工智能的基础设施可能会给电网和当地供水系统带来压力的抗议。造成这种情况的部分原因是人们担心了解它们实际上消耗了多少电力或水是多么困难。加州的新披露规则不会提供全面的信息，但从明年开始，数据中心运营商将不得不开始分享其中一些细节。透明度将帮助科学家和公众了解数据中心是否增加了费用、耗尽了日益减少的资源以及兑现了可持续发展承诺。
“试图了解基本信息是非常令人沮丧的，”忧思科学家联盟 (UCS) 气候和能源项目高级经理马克·斯佩赫特 (Mark Specht) 说。 “现在有很多关于数据中心的炒作……我们只是没有关于数据中心发生的情况的基本事实，无法尝试了解它们的问题有多大，这无济于事。”
“这非常令人沮丧”
纽瑟姆签署的七项法案超出了要求披露的范围。参议院第 886 号法案、众议院第 2383 号法案和参议院第 1168 号法案指示加州公用事业委员会为数据中心制定单独的电价，以补偿将此类耗电设施连接到电网的成本。这应该可以防止数据中心将成本转嫁给为满足能源需求而建造的新基础设施的其他消费者。除此之外，AB 2383 还推动数据中心使用更多的可再生能源。
立法的其余部分旨在解决公众在数据中心如何影响周围社区和环境方面存在的巨大差距。 AB 1577 要求每月报告数据中心的能源消耗。 AB 2619 和 AB 2469 要求披露水信息，后者还要求数据中心运营商负责承担为其提供服务所需的基础设施升级成本。 SB 887 取消了《加州环境质量法案》对数据中心的绝对豁免，确保它们接受环境审查。
“作为科学家，当我们前往加利福尼亚州进行研究时，我对缺乏可利用的信息感到有点沮丧。所以我很高兴 [AB 1577] 通过了，”Specht 说。
今年，斯佩希特与他人共同撰写了一份情况说明书，介绍数据中心如何影响加州的电网和公用事业费率。它描述了一种情景，其中多种因素推高了加州人的成本：电力需求不断膨胀；需要昂贵的新基础设施来将数据中心连接到高压传输系统；如果人工智能泡沫破灭并且数据中心最终没有使用预期那么多的电力，那么就会面临过度建设的风险，而其他公用事业客户则要为此买单。
另一种情况表明数据中心实际上可以降低电力成本
另一方面，另一种情况表明数据中心实际上可以降低电力成本。电费包括电网维护的固定成本，因此将这些成本分摊给更多客户可以降低每个人的电费。问题是，潜在的节省取决于数据中心对整个配电系统成本的贡献，该系统以较低的电压为较小的客户提供服务。大型数据中心通常通过连接到传输高压电力的传输系统来避免这些成本。
如果没有更多信息，就不可能判断加州正在形成哪种情况。 “我不会明确地说数据中心增加了[电力]成本，”斯佩希特说。 “他们甚至可能已经击倒了一些人，我只是认为我们没有足够的数据来证明这一点。”
斯佩希特补充道，即使数据中心还没有对电费产生太大影响，但随着电力需求的增长，情况也可能会发生变化，这使得了解他们使用了多少能源变得更加重要。他告诉 The Verge：“我们要做的只是在我们都开始感受到它之前先行一步。”
数据中心的用水情况同样不透明。在研究数据中心对加利福尼亚州缺水社区的影响时，圣克拉拉大学的研究人员最近联系了数据中心所在地区的每个供水提供商。每个地区的供应商都以隐私法规为由，拒绝分享数据中心用水量的数据。研究人员还发现，该州很少有数据中心向公众提供环境影响报告。
法律在数据中心需要报告的内容方面仍然存在很大差距
考虑到研究人员能够找到的内容，信息的缺乏更令人担忧。随着人工智能推动超大规模数据中心的发展，这些设施正从更富裕的城市地区转移到更多的农村地区，在这些地区，小型供水系统和低收入社区可能更难以应对增加的需求。
这些法律在数据中心需要报告的内容方面仍然存在很大差距。具体来说，AB 2619 和 AB 2469 仅要求公司在申请许可证或获得营业执照时披露用水量，因此我们无法知道他们每年实际使用了多少水。他们分享用水量的年份可能特别潮湿或凉爽，并不一定反映设施在炎热和干燥时需要多少水。它还使得很难看出数据中心的消耗是否在增长，或者公司是否正在实现其可持续发展目标。
尽管如此，“这在很多方面都是朝着正确方向迈出的一步。它向业界发出信号，表明人们正在关注，立法者正在关注，”该水报告的主要作者、圣克拉拉大学环境科学教授艾里斯·斯图尔特-弗雷说。
她指出，纽瑟姆去年实际上否决了类似的水披露法案，但从那时起，数据中心已成为公众更大的担忧。
“整个人工智能浪潮不是自然力量，也不是飓风，”她说。 “这是我们实际上可以监管的事情。”
